report:
## Conclusion

**Yes—on balance, offering HIV self-testing *in addition to* standard testing increases the number of people who test for HIV.** The strongest evidence is systematic-review evidence from randomized trials rather than a single study.

A 2021 systematic review/meta-analysis of 13 randomized controlled trials found that HIV self-testing increased testing uptake overall (risk ratio **2.09**, 95% CI 1.69–2.58; **moderate-certainty** evidence). This means uptake was roughly twice as high in self-testing strategies as in the comparison testing services, though the absolute increase will differ by population, setting, price, delivery method, and how easy conventional testing already is. https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2589537021002716

A separate systematic review, also drawing on randomized trials, estimated a smaller but still clear relative increase—**1.45 times** as many people tested with HIV self-testing than with standard services. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7713313/

The evidence is not uniformly strong in every context. For **facility-based** self-testing specifically, WHO says uptake may be *comparable to or higher than* standard facility testing—so simply placing self-tests in a clinic may not always add much where ordinary testing is already convenient. https://www.who.int/news/item/22-07-2023-who-recommends-optimizing-hiv-testing-services

Important qualification: more testing does not automatically ensure equivalent follow-up. One review found a possible reduction in linkage to HIV care/treatment after a reactive self-test versus standard testing, although estimates varied. Programs should therefore provide clear confirmatory-testing and care-linkage support. https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0245498
